work.title: Plato, Apology
work.notes: Socrates wrote no philosophical works. The Apology is Plato's literary representation of his defence; preserve Plato's authorship and distinguish dramatic speech from a verbatim trial transcript.

passages.translationText: Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,—for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.
passages.interpretiveNote: Socratic human wisdom consists in not adding a false claim of knowledge to one's ignorance. The passage does not mean that Socrates knows literally nothing or that ignorance itself is sufficient wisdom.
passages.period: Platonic representation of Socrates; historical English translation

passages.translationText: You, my friend,—a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens,—are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honour and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul, which you never regard or heed at all?
passages.interpretiveNote: The challenge reorders priorities: care of wisdom, truth, character, and soul precedes the accumulation of wealth and reputation. It is a call to examination, not contempt for every material need.
passages.period: Platonic representation of Socrates; historical English translation

passages.translationText: daily to discourse about virtue, and of those other things about which you hear me examining myself and others, is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living
passages.interpretiveNote: The examined life is an ongoing practice of dialogue and self-testing. The famous line should not be used to declare another person's life worthless or to intensify distress.
